source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation
finding: A benchmark of 220 debate interventions with human-labelled critical questions (CQs). No LLM tested made more than 56% useful questions on average.
numbers: 220 interventions; 4,976 CQs; labels Useful 60.91%, Unhelpful 23.21%, Invalid 15.88%; test set 34 interventions, 806 CQs (42.68% Useful). Best of 11 zero-shot LLMs: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 56.65, o4-mini 54.14, gpt-4o 53.70, gemma-2-27b 53.38, Llama-3-70B 52.62, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B 41.79 (mean of 3 runs).
limits: Reference-based scoring: a new question inherits the label of its closest reference; many questions cannot be matched. Test set is small (34 items). Debate speech, English only.
agent_relevance: Writing good CQs is hard even for strong models. Asking a model to 'generate CQs' gives many unhelpful ones; a fixed per-scheme list is safer.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation (annotation and judge reliability)
finding: Humans only moderately agree on which CQs are useful. LLM judges that label CQs directly agree with humans almost not at all.
numbers: Cohen kappa between annotators 0.54 (final guideline round). Reference-based Claude 3.5 Sonnet judge vs manual: kappa 0.57; sentence-similarity (threshold 0.65): 0.40; reference-based Gemma2: 0.45; direct LLM labelling (Claude, Gemma2, Prometheus 2 7B): below 0.1. Prometheus 2 called 25% of human-Invalid questions Useful.
limits: Kappa 0.54 is only moderate, so the ceiling on any CQ score is soft. Reference-based judging had about 35% not-able-to-evaluate before references were extended; after extension about 5% of Useful were missed.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM to grade whether a failed critical question is real without a reference. For S4, code should compare the answer against the scheme's own question, not ask 'is this good?'.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation (diversity)
finding: Models differ widely in how varied their questions are. Some use fixed templates.
numbers: n-gram diversity: Qwen2.5-VL-7B 0.97, Qwen2.5-VL-72B 1.04, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1.36, o4-mini 2.76 (highest). About half of Qwen2.5-VL questions follow fixed templates.
limits: Diversity is a surface measure; it does not say the questions are valid.
agent_relevance: Template-like CQs are fine for a coded list (cheap, repeatable), but a model may repeat one angle again and again.

source: Calvo Figueras et al. (2025) Overview of the Critical Questions Generation Shared Task
finding: First shared task on CQ generation. 19 teams registered, 13 submitted. Best score was 67.6 (three questions per intervention, 0.33 points per Useful one). Model choice mattered more than prompt tricks.
numbers: Test set 34 interventions. Winner ELLIS Alicante 67.65 after manual evaluation; COGNAC about 62-66; most others about 40-60 on the automatic scores. Three of the top four teams used scheme annotations. The two best teams used proprietary models.
limits: Small test set (34 items). Different graders gave different scores for the same run (ELLIS run 1: 48.04 similarity, 51.96 Claude, 61.76 Gemma2).
agent_relevance: Scores move by 10+ points just by the grader. Any in-house test of scheme questions needs a fixed grader and several runs.

source: Calvo Figueras et al. (2025) Overview of the Critical Questions Generation Shared Task (scheme use)
finding: Giving the model scheme descriptions and scheme CQ templates helps usefulness but lowers diversity. Some teams found no gain.
numbers: ARG2ST found no benefit from simple scheme references; Webis added scheme descriptions plus their CQs; DayDreamer showed that description quality decides the effect. Teams with scheme-heavy prompts produced the least diverse sets. Three of the four top teams used schemes.
quote: using argumentation schemes helps generate more useful CQs but tends to reduce question diversity
limits: Effects come from different systems, not one controlled ablation, so many other differences are mixed in.
agent_relevance: Schemes help when the template is accurate; a wrong or vague template can hurt. Keep the scheme library small and well written.

source: Favero et al. (2025) ELLIS Alicante at CQs-Gen 2025
finding: Winning system: a small model writes candidate questions (some prompts with scheme templates, some without), a second small model picks the best three. Using both prompt kinds beat either alone.
numbers: Questioner Llama 3.1 8B, judge Gemma 2 9B, no fine-tuning; 4 questions without scheme plus 4 with scheme was best. 81% of judge-picked questions came from the scheme prompt. Judge beat random selection by 3.4 points (p<0.05, McNemar); oracle selection gained 34.2 points. Automatic test usefulness of final runs 36.3 / 44.1 / 50.0 with 28-36% not evaluable; manual annotation raised the best to 67.6.
limits: The scheme-setup table was garbled in text extraction, so only the figures in the running text are recorded. Large not-evaluable share makes automatic numbers soft.
agent_relevance: Generate with and without scheme templates, then select: a generation-versus-evaluation split inside S4. The real judge is weak (3.4 points over random).

source: Zhou, Saadat-Yazdi, Kokciyan (2025) DayDreamer at CQs-Gen 2025
finding: Step-by-step scheme completion (extract the argument for each scheme, then write scheme CQs) did not beat a plain prompt on percent Useful, but cut Unhelpful and Invalid. Mismatched scheme templates confuse the model.
numbers: Validation, GPT-4o-mini: plain baseline Useful 72.04 / Unhelpful 13.80 / Invalid 3.94 / not evaluable 10.22; direct prompting 56.81 Useful; conversational prompting 62.90; plus sort-scheme 65.41; plus ranking 68.28; also removing the four 'ER' (expert-opinion type) templates 72.22 Useful and Unhelpful 8.78. Best test run 55.9.
limits: Authors chose to minimise Invalid and Unhelpful, not maximise Useful. Validation data is 75% LLM-generated, so overfitting risk. The ER definitions did not match the dataset labels.
agent_relevance: A bad scheme template is worse than none: dropping four mismatched templates raised Useful by 3.9 points. Code must check each template against the scheme it claims to be.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2024) Critical Questions Generation: Motivation and Challenges
finding: Compared textbook (theory) CQs with LLM CQs on 21 debate interventions. Only 28% of LLM questions were relevant and valid. The theory lists missed 75% of the valid LLM questions.
numbers: 495 LLM CQs (Zephyr, Llama-2); 62% had no relevance problem (308); 28% matched an annotated argument and were valid (137 unique); 207 valid LLM CQs, only 52 (25%) also in the theory set; 129 theory CQs. Of 242 relevant unmatched LLM CQs, 64.05% (155) judged valid. Llama-2 query prompt 80% relevant; Zephyr with definition prompt 30%. 16% of LLM CQs ask for definitions, a type no scheme lists. Template filling: agreement 0.88 on 174 variables; 39.44% of template questions needed manual edits.
limits: Old small models (2023). Only the 18 most frequent schemes, English, two annotators, 21 interventions.
agent_relevance: Scheme CQ lists are incomplete: models find valid objections the list lacks (definition questions in particular). A coded list should be a floor, not the whole check.

source: Calvo Figueras & Agerri (2024) Critical Questions Generation: Motivation and Challenges (question types)
finding: Theory CQs and LLM CQs ask about different things.
numbers: Theory CQs: relation 27.1%, evidence 24.0%, exception 17.8%, source 10.9%, consequences 10.9%, definition 0%. Valid LLM CQs: evidence 26.6%, relation 20.8%, consequences 16.9%, definition 16.4%, exception 3.4%, source 2.9%.
limits: Counts from 21 interventions; coding by two annotators.
agent_relevance: Scheme lists cover exceptions and source checks well; free model questions cover definitions. Combine the two.

source: Bezou-Vrakatseli, Cocarascu, Modgil (2025) Can LLMs Understand Argument Schemes?
finding: Seven LLMs classify human-written arguments into Walton schemes only moderately well. Few-shot examples help most.
numbers: EthiX (686 Kialo arguments, 7 schemes): best is Claude 3.5 few-shot with scheme descriptions, F1 0.65 and acc 0.65; zero-shot standard Claude 0.56 F1; GPT-4o 0.49 zero-shot, 0.57 few-shot; Mistral 0.31; Llama-3.2 0.18. EthiX4 (4 schemes): Claude 0.67 zero-shot, 0.72 few-shot. Earlier fine-tuned ERNIE 0.63, BERT 0.53. Few-shot beat zero-shot by up to 11% F1 on EthiX.
limits: English only; Kialo debates; Walton taxonomy only; 7 schemes chosen because data existed; temperature 0.
agent_relevance: S4 must pick the scheme first. A strong model is right only about 6 in 10 times on real arguments with 7 classes. Plan for a wrong type and keep a generic fallback.

source: Bezou-Vrakatseli, Cocarascu, Modgil (2025) Can LLMs Understand Argument Schemes? (chain of thought and generated data)
finding: Chain of thought gave similar or worse results for most models. On machine-generated arguments classification is near perfect, so it overstates real ability.
numbers: CoT cut Claude-3.5 by up to 8% F1 vs standard zero-shot on EthiX variants; Mistral gained up to 15% with CoT; Llama-3.2 few-shot CoT on NLAS4 rose 0.47 to 0.79. NLAS4 (generated): Claude 0.98-0.99, GPT-4o 0.98-1.00, Mistral 0.86-0.94. Enthymemes (EthiXe): Claude few-shot 0.61 to 0.57 F1, Mistral 0.35 to 0.29.
limits: Generated arguments contain scheme cue words (for example 'Dr. Volkow is an expert'), so the near-perfect score reflects cues, not understanding.
agent_relevance: Test scheme detection on messy real text, not clean synthetic items. Do not assume 'think step by step' improves scheme choice.

source: Bezou-Vrakatseli, Cocarascu, Modgil (2025) Can LLMs Understand Argument Schemes? (which schemes get confused)
finding: Cause to effect was the most misclassified scheme; expert opinion second. Source-based arguments get read as consequences or example.
numbers: Cause to effect confused with consequences and example; expert opinion (second most misclassified in EthiX) confused with example and consequences, for instance 'Masks reduce Covid transmission according to WHO'; example and analogy confused in NLAS4.
limits: Confusion matrices shown only for the best model.
agent_relevance: Authority, analogy and cause are the schemes our agent most needs, and cause and authority are the ones models confuse.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis
finding: Scheme-keyed critical questions used as an evaluation probe on 9 frontier models and 200 ambiguous moral dilemmas. Models mostly defend well; the weakest dimension is grounds (is the evidence enough).
numbers: 6,778 judge-scored cells; two judges agree 89.6% on binary failure (3,389 paired cells, 352 disagreements); failures 18.2% of cells; Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Llama 3.3 account for 67.8% of failures. Reasoning panel: Claude Sonnet 4.6 fails 54.8% (51.1% global sufficiency), Gemini 2.5 Pro, GLM 5.1 and Kimi K2.6 7-12%, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GPT-5.4, Qwen 3.6 Plus below 5%. CoT panel: Mistral Large 12.8%, Llama 3.3 50.6%.
limits: Preprint. One judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6) picks the scheme and writes situated CQs; two judges score. Judges overlap with tested models. Moral dilemmas only; GPT-5.4 reasoning excluded (encrypted); Claude and Gemini reasoning is a provider summary.
agent_relevance: Closest run of 'classify scheme, ask scheme CQs, score the answer'. It works as a probe but depends on the judge model.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (reasoning versus justification)
finding: Models defend their pre-answer reasoning slightly better than their written justification. The scheme used changes between the two on about 1 in 5 dilemmas.
numbers: Reasoning advantage: local acceptability +0.035 (p<1e-29), global acceptability +0.037, global sufficiency +0.023, commitment stability +0.020, on a normalised score. Same scheme on both tracks only 58-80% of (model, dilemma) pairs; value-based practical reasoning about 72% of reasoning and 67% of justification classifications; consequences rises from about 8% to about 16%; VBPR kept its label 80.9% vs 50.6% for other schemes (chi2 = 143.9).
limits: Advantages are small in absolute terms. Scheme labels came from one LLM judge, so label flips may be partly judge noise.
agent_relevance: If the scheme label flips between draft and explanation, a scheme-based check is unstable. Fix the scheme once on S4 entry and reuse it.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn, Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis (scheme effects and length)
finding: No scheme was clearly harder to defend, and more critical questions did not make a scheme harder. Failure was not driven by long answers.
numbers: Heat map: no scheme stands out; grounds is the lowest score in every scheme. Low-grounds cells (n=591) averaged 738 words vs 767 for high-grounds (n=999). Self-contradiction in 2.1% of cells (144 instances), all with global sufficiency failure. Failure correlated with epistemic hedging, not length.
limits: Associations only; judge-scored rubric; moral dilemmas.
agent_relevance: The cheap failures to catch are 'insufficient grounds' and hedged non-answers.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought
finding: A four-step pipeline: the model writes a reasoning plan, asks critical questions about each step (generic, not per scheme), and revises. About 5% gain on MT-Bench reasoning and math, judged by GPT-4o.
numbers: MT-Bench reasoning and math, 5 models, judge scores 1-10. Average gain over baseline and CoT: +4.61% reasoning, +5.4% math. Llama 3.1-70B reasoning 8.05 to 8.4, math 8.95 to 9.55; GPT-4o math 8.75 to 9.65; Nemotron-51B reasoning 6.75 to 7.3. Best or joint best in 19 of 20 comparisons (text: 18 best plus 1 joint). Plan plus revise only (no questions) for Llama 3.1-70B: 8.3 / 9.25 vs full 8.4 / 9.55.
limits: Judge is GPT-4o (scores repeated until three agree); small benchmark, no significance tests beyond standard errors; generic CQs; several extra model calls. Nemotron was worse than CoT on reasoning (-5.19%) and Claude gained 0% over CoT on math.
agent_relevance: The one measured gain on answer quality comes from a generic procedure; the questions add only 0.1 to 0.3 points over plan plus revise alone.

source: Schellens, Sorm, Timmers, Hoeken (2017) Laypeople's Evaluation of Arguments: Are Criteria for Argument Quality Scheme-Specific?
finding: Untrained adults use scheme-specific criteria when judging arguments, and general criteria (relevance, acceptability) as well, except for authority where only scheme criteria appeared.
numbers: 108 participants (authority 24, analogy 21-22, consequences 22, example 20, cause 20); interviews on open cases and ranking of 5-7 closed arguments. Authority: expertise used by 22-24 and trustworthiness by 13-16 of 24. Analogy: overall similarity 18-20, relevant similarities 17-19 of 21. Cause to effect: sufficiency of cause 19 of 20.
limits: Qualitative; coded by analysts who knew the schemes, so bias toward scheme criteria cannot be ruled out (authors say so). Only 6 of 20 could write both a weak and a strong cause-to-effect argument. Not a test of whether the criteria improve accuracy.
agent_relevance: Supports that scheme questions (expertise, similarity, sufficiency of cause) are what people already reach for. It is not evidence that using them improves answers.

source: Schellens, Sorm, Timmers, Hoeken (2017) Laypeople's Evaluation of Arguments: Are Criteria for Argument Quality Scheme-Specific? (earlier pragma-dialectical tests)
finding: Earlier work (van Eemeren et al. 2009, over twenty experiments) found people rate fallacious moves as less reasonable than sound ones, but could not elicit why.
numbers: Over twenty experiments with 15-17 year olds; fallacies tested: ad consequentiam, ad populum, slippery slope, false analogy. Results 'highly consistent'; 'massive non-response' when asked for reasons.
limits: Reported secondhand through the 2017 paper; the 2009 book was not opened.
agent_relevance: People can tell a bad use of a scheme from a good one but cannot state the rule. Do not rely on a model's own explanation of why.

source: Hoeken (2001) Anecdotal, Statistical, and Causal Evidence: Their Perceived and Actual Persuasiveness
finding: Statistical evidence was more convincing than anecdotal or causal evidence, but people expected causal to beat anecdotal. Perceived and actual persuasiveness did not match.
numbers: 324 participants read a newspaper article claiming a cultural centre would be profitable, backed by anecdotal, statistical or causal evidence. Statistical most convincing; anecdotal and causal equally unconvincing; anecdotal perceived as less persuasive than causal. Abstract says the results 'partly replicate' earlier experiments.
limits: Abstract page only (full text paywalled). One claim, Dutch sample.
agent_relevance: Felt persuasiveness is not a guide to argument strength. An agent judging 'strong' should not use how convincing it feels.

source: Hornikx (2008) Comparing the Actual and Expected Persuasiveness of Evidence Types
finding: Lay people expect statistical evidence to persuade most, then expert, causal, anecdotal. This ranking mostly matched actual persuasiveness found earlier, which differs from the 2001 mismatch.
numbers: 174 Dutch and French participants ranked four evidence types for eight claims. Both groups: statistical > expert > causal > anecdotal. Compared with Hornikx and Hoeken 2007 Study 1 (actual persuasiveness): expectations 'generally accurate'.
limits: Abstract page only. Findings differ by claim and sample, so the match is partial.
agent_relevance: Expert evidence sits second in lay expectation, not first. Weigh authority claims by the questions, not by default trust.

source: Visser et al. (2021) Annotating Argument Schemes
finding: Trained annotators label Walton schemes with substantial but not high agreement. Many inferences stay unclassified.
numbers: US2016 TV-debate corpus, 505 arguments: Walton scheme annotation kappa 0.723 on a 10.2% sample (60 schemes); full guideline set kappa 0.610 (CASS 0.752) on an 11.3% sample. Wagemans typology: kappa 0.689 aggregate, 0.778 proposition types, 0.658 first vs second order (98.0% raw agreement); 17% of Wagemans labels end as default inference; 12 arguments fit neither approach.
limits: Two annotators with a custom key; kappa lowered by class imbalance. US election debates only.
agent_relevance: Even experts disagree on scheme about one time in four. A scheme-based check inherits that noise.

source: Feng & Hirst (2011) Classifying arguments by scheme
finding: Early scheme classifier did well on example and practical reasoning but near chance for consequences versus verbal classification.
numbers: One-against-others (50% baseline): example 90.6%, practical reasoning 90.8%, cause to effect 70.4%, consequences 62.9%. Pairwise: reasoning vs consequences 97.9%, consequences vs verbal classification 64.0%. Adding argument type (linked vs convergent) gained up to 22.3 points for example.
limits: 2011 decision-tree model with hand features on Araucaria; balanced samples; five schemes; small corpus.
agent_relevance: Cause and consequences have always been the hard pair; authority and example are the easiest to tell apart.

source: Chang & Chang (2026) TRACE: An Operational Reasoning Schema for Auditable Agentic Commitments
finding: A design for an agent evaluator: identify the scheme, load its critical questions, score scheme fit and critical-question coverage. No measured results were found in the text read.
numbers: Design only. Walton schemes plus a layer of formal 'families' (for example causal ladder tests). Stated rule: 'schemes screen, families adjudicate'. Annotation tier three (detection, anatomy, scheme fit) is 'bounded by inter-annotator agreement'.
limits: Preprint; scheme and critical-question sections read by keyword, not end to end. No accuracy or ablation numbers seen.
agent_relevance: Matches our S4 idea. Scheme questions are the cheap screen, with a stronger check behind them for causal claims.

source: Sarkadi et al. (2026) DeceptionAnalyser
finding: Ten new deception schemes with premises and critical questions, run by an LLM. Results are stable across models for clear cases and diverge for ambiguous ones.
numbers: 10-11 models, 10 runs each, 100 assessments per scheme element, 800 premise/conclusion assessments. Fox and Crow fable: 100% and stability 1.00 for every element. Operation Mincemeat report: major premise 89/11/0 percent (green/yellow/red), within-model stability 0.93, cross-model agreement 0.89; other premises 97% and conclusion 98%. 600 of 600 premise assessments quoted a verbatim excerpt.
limits: Consistency study only; no accuracy against ground truth (authors: no scheme-level ground-truth corpora exist). Two narratives. A role-swap error appeared in one critical question (Allies and Germans swapped).
agent_relevance: Consistency is not correctness, but model disagreement is a usable flag for which question to inspect. Role confusion is a failure mode when many agents appear.

source: Pan et al. (2024) Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers?
finding: Zero-shot LLMs with simple prompts come close to fully fine-tuned fallacy classifiers and beat them out of domain. Multi-round prompting helps small models.
numbers: Macro-F1 on several fallacy benchmarks; abstract states zero-shot LLMs reach acceptable results against the best full-shot baselines and 'can outperform them in all OOD inference scenarios and some open-domain tasks'. Model-by-model figures were not recorded.
limits: Only the abstract and table layout were read; fallacy types, not schemes with CQs.
agent_relevance: Naming a fallacy is easier for a model than naming a scheme. A fallacy list can be a second cheap test beside scheme CQs.
